query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) such as WTaMoNbV can be used to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix due to its excellent wear resistance and high thermal stability.
generation.intervention: Adhering a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) such as WTaMoNbV to the surface of the Cu matrix
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a stable, protective oxide film via tribo-oxidation
generation.mechanism: The RHEA's high entropy and refractory nature allow it to form a stable oxide film, which protects the underlying Cu matrix from wear and corrosion
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance and surface protection of the Cu matrix
generation.boundary: Temperature and wear conditions beyond which the RHEA coating becomes ineffective
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and processing conditions of the RHEA required to achieve optimal adhesion and wear resistance

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative wear resistance test between Cu matrix with and without RHEA coating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RHEA-coated Cu matrix shows no significant improvement in wear resistance compared to the uncoated Cu matrix, the hypothesis is falsified

Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite processing challenges, and how do its microstructure, hardness, and corrosion resistance compare to traditional superalloys and arc-melted counterparts?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition of Nb, Mo, Ta, W powders with 99.9% purity). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); parameters included hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, and a triple-pass remelting strategy (3x energy input) to achieve a linear energy density of 2.83 J/mm. Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C. Test conditions: Reciprocating wear test using an SRV-Tribometer with a force of 26 N, frequency of 40 Hz, amplitude of 0.5 mm, and Al2O3 counter body (10 mm diameter) at temperatures of 22 °C, 500 °C, 650 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C for 900 s. Question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?. System: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at.% W, 20 at.% Ta, 20 at.% Mo, 20 at.% Nb, 20 at.% V). Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system (400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere); mixed elemental powders (20–70 µm) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; advanced trials parameters: 244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 0.10 mm hatch spacing, 0.03 mm layer thickness, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density, 67° layer rotation.. Test conditions: Density and Vickers hardness (HV10) measured; compression strength tested at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; electrochemical behavior assessed via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (scanning rate 0.5 mV/s)..
